o: We remove elements from the end one at a time and stop as soon as our collection contains every value 1..k. In example 1 ([3,1,5,4,2], k=2) popping gives 2,4,5,1 — after 4 pops we have both 1 and 2. The constraints are tiny (n ≤ 50), so any linear scan works; the interesting part is tracking 'have I seen all of 1..k' cheaply.
k: Scan from the right; the answer is the index where the set of collected values ≤ k first reaches size k.
A bitmask of k bits (or a boolean array) tracks coverage in O(1) per element.

a.n: Approach 1: Backward Scan with Hash Set
a.i: Pop from the end conceptually, adding values ≤ k to a set; the moment the set has k distinct values we are done, and the number of pops equals n minus the current index.
s: Iterate i from n-1 down to 0.
If nums[i] <= k add it to a set.
When the set size hits k, return n - i.
a.t: O(n) — single backward pass with O(1) set operations
a.sp: O(k) — the set holds at most k values

a.i: Since values are bounded by k ≤ n ≤ 50, an integer bitmask encodes which of 1..k were collected; coverage is complete when the mask equals 2^k − 1. This avoids hashing entirely.
s: Set bit nums[i]-1 when nums[i] <= k.
Stop when mask == (1<<k)-1 and return n - i.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with bitwise updates

w: Either approach is fine given n ≤ 50; mention the bitmask as the elegant O(1)-space variant. Pitfall: values greater than k should be ignored, not treated as failures. A follow-up might ask for huge k, where the set version still works.
